raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old Caucasian female presented to the emergency department with complaints of increasing lethargy and fatigue over the course of several weeks, along with a one-day history of shortness of breath, hematemesis, and palpitations. Past medical history was significant for HIV, anemia, and septoplasty. She was intubated on admission for airway protection due to concern for impending respiratory failure. On exam she was found to be febrile with Tmax of 39.9C, heart rate of 122 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 91/57 mmHg, saturating at 97% on 35% FiO2. Complete blood count revealed white blood cells of 3 x 103 cells/mL with 73% segs and 15% bands, hemoglobin of 4.5 g/dL, hematocrit of 17.7%, and platelets of 4,000 cells/mL. Ferritin was significantly elevated at 19,406 ng/mL and triglycerides were 412 mg/dL. HIV viral load was 1,842,730 copies/mL and CD4 count was 4 cells/mL. Physical exam revealed hepatosplenomegaly which was confirmed by abdominal ultrasound. The patient was diagnosed with HLH based on meeting the required five of eight criteria set forth in HLH-2004 guidelines (fever > 38.5C, splenomegaly, bicytopenia with hemoglobin < 9 g/dL and platelets < 100,000 cells/mL, triglycerides > 265 mg/dL, and ferritin > 500 ng/mL). The other three criteria (NK cell activity, CD25 level, and pathological evidence of hemophagocytosis) were not evaluated due to unavailability of labs and thrombocytopenia precluding bone marrow biopsy.
The patient was placed on empirical antibiotics (levofloxacin and vancomycin) for sepsis while investigation for infectious source was conducted. She was also started on methylprednisolone for respiratory failure at admission, which was continued for three days. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Sputum culture grew normal flora. Tests were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid fast bacilli, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, cryptococcus, histoplasmosis, syphilis, and influenza A. The only positive finding was antibody for influenza B, which was attributed to a mild upper respiratory infection that had resolved on its own with supportive measures two weeks prior to admission.
Despite aggressive transfusions, significant anemia and thrombocytopenia persisted. At this point, the most likely trigger of the HLH was determined to be an uncontrolled HIV infection. Given the patient's clinical instability and unresponsiveness to supportive treatment, ART was empirically initiated with tenofovir/emtricitabine, darunavir, and ritonavir. Within one week of initiation of ART, the patient improved clinically and was able to be extubated, and her laboratory parameters began to normalize (Figure 1). By the time the patient was discharged three weeks after ART initiation, hemoglobin had risen to 10.5 g/dL and platelets to 169,000 cells/mL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old female presenting with progressive lethargy and fatigue for several weeks, and acute shortness of breath, hematemesis, and palpitations for one day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a multi-week history of worsening fatigue and lethargy, culminating in acute respiratory distress, hematemesis, and palpitations on the day of admission. Due to hemodynamic instability and impending respiratory failure, she was endotracheally intubated in the emergency department for airway protection. Her clinical course was complicated by refractory bicytopenia and extreme hyperferritinemia requiring massive blood product transfusions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (uncontrolled/non-adherent); history of chronic anemia; prior septoplasty.
subjective.review_of_systems: Profound lethargy, fatigue, dyspnea, hematemesis, palpitations, and fever; denies antecedent jaundice, rash, seizures, or focal weakness. History of mild self-limiting upper respiratory infection two weeks prior.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals on mechanical ventilation: Temperature 39.9 °C, heart rate 122 beats/min (tachycardia), respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, blood pressure 91/57 mmHg (hypotension), oxygen saturation 97% on 35% FiO2. General: Intubated, sedated, acutely ill. Abdomen: Palpable hepatosplenomegaly without localized peritonitis.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: White blood cells 3.0 x 10^3/microL (neutrophils 73%, bands 15%), hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL, hematocrit 17.7%, platelet count 4,000/microL (severe bicytopenia). Metabolic & Inflammatory: Serum ferritin 19,406 ng/mL, fasting serum triglycerides 412 mg/dL. Bedside abdominal ultrasound: Confirmed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Infectious workup: Blood, urine, and sputum bacterial cultures were negative; diagnostic workup negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, acid-fast bacilli, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus B19, Epstein-Barr virus, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Treponema pallidum, and influenza A; serology positive for influenza B IgG/antibodies.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS; CD4 count 4 cells/microL, HIV-1 RNA viral load 1,842,730 copies/mL) presenting with primary HIV-induced hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; fulfilled 5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria: fever > 38.5 °C, splenomegaly, severe bicytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperferritinemia > 19,000 ng/mL), complicated by upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with mechanical ventilation, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (IV vancomycin and levofloxacin), IV methylprednisolone for 3 days, and aggressive packed red blood cell and platelet transfusions. Following exclusion of secondary opportunistic and malignant triggers, antiretroviral therapy was urgently initiated with tenofovir/emtricitabine, darunavir, and ritonavir. Marked clinical and hematological recovery occurred within 7 days, permitting successful extubation. By week 3 post-ART initiation, the patient was discharged with hemoglobin improved to 10.5 g/dL and platelet count normalized to 169,000/microL.
